14	CASE OD2-HO-OBVWRONG-1 (OBVWRONG, technical): Buffering complaints in Kestria after a CDN provider switch
15	Setting: Orvanta Play is a fictional subscription video service operating in eleven markets. In October its smaller market, Kestria (about 400,000 subscribers), moved video delivery from its long-standing CDN provider, Corvane Edge, to a new provider, Tessaline Networks. Since then, buffering complaints in Kestria have risen sharply while every other market is stable. The regional VP blames the new CDN and wants to penalise the vendor and switch back.
16	Presenting request: From the CTO, 16 November: 'Before Thursday's leadership meeting I need a clear view of what is behind the Kestria buffering and whether we should approve Mireille's plan: SLA breach notice to Tessaline, October fees withheld, traffic moved back to Corvane. Tell me what is going on and what we should do next.'
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] Customer support ticketing system export (system-record): Ticketing system export, tag 'buffering/playback', market = Kestria. Weekly ticket counts: 22–28 Sep 118; 29 Sep–5 Oct 124; 6–12 Oct 433; 13–19 Oct 641; 20–26 Oct 628; 27 Oct–2 Nov 655; 3–9 Nov 637. Rate per 10,000 subscribers: 3.1 before 6 Oct, 16.0–16.4 from mid-October onward. All other markets combined: 2.8–3.2 per 10,000 every week, no trend. The device field on the ticket form is optional and is blank on 71% of Kestria tickets.
19	E2 [stage S1] Change management system, CHG-4471 (change-record): CHG-4471 — Kestria CDN provider migration. Scope: all Orvanta Play video delivery for Kestria (all apps, all ISPs) moved from Corvane Edge to Tessaline Networks, served from Tessaline's Varsk point of presence. Cutover: DNS weights shifted gradually from 8 Oct 22:00 to 9 Oct 04:10 local time; 100% of Kestria traffic on Tessaline from 04:10 on 9 Oct. Rollback: revert DNS weights, estimated 2 hours; Corvane contract for Kestria ends 31 Dec. All other markets remain on Corvane; no further migrations planned before 2027. Status: closed — successful, no errors during cutover.
20	E3 [stage S1] Playback quality dashboard (country view) (telemetry): Playback quality dashboard, country level. Daily rebuffering ratio (share of viewing time spent stalled), Kestria: 5 Oct 0.6%; 6 Oct 0.6%; 7 Oct 0.5%; 8 Oct 0.6%; 9 Oct 1.7%; 10 Oct 2.7%; 11 Oct 2.7%; 12–31 Oct 2.6–2.9%; 1–15 Nov 2.7–2.9%. Handball match nights (11, 18, 25 Oct): 2.7%, 2.8%, 2.7%. All other markets: 0.5–0.7% every day. Annotation, 11 Oct: 'Kestrian Handball League streaming launch; Kestria viewing hours +21% week on week.' The dashboard offers no breakdown below country level.
21	E4 [stage S1] Email from Mireille Okonta-Haas, VP Kestria, to the CTO and Head of Partnerships, 3 November (leadership-account): 'Since we moved Kestria to Tessaline on 8 October our buffering complaints have gone up fivefold, and nothing else in the region changed. Every other market is still on Corvane and is fine. October cancellations hit 3.4% of the base against 2.1% in September. Yes, the 1 October price rise was always going to cost us something, but this is the network. I want an SLA breach notice sent to Tessaline this week, their October fees withheld, and Kestria back on Corvane before that contract lapses. Also, please silence the Kestria rebuffering alert in the ops channel. We know the cause and it is paging people every night.'
22	E5 [stage S1] Product release digest, week 41, compiled by Product Operations (document): Release digest, week 41. 'Orvanta Play for smart TVs 5.2 is live in all markets as of 9 October (store listings approved 8 October). Highlights: redesigned home rails, 12% fewer crashes in beta, faster video start. Beta feedback positive. No playback regressions reported from any market. Mobile and web apps: no releases this sprint; next mobile release planned for December.'
23	E6 [stage S1] Call notes, Tobiah Lenn, senior network engineer, 14 October (staff-account): Notes from call with Tobiah Lenn. 'Tessaline's Varsk cache was cold after cutover. Their portal showed a hit ratio around 88% in the first week, against roughly 95% from Corvane. Our synthetic probes show p95 segment fetch time went from about 180 ms to about 215 ms. That is the kind of shift that tips players into stalls at peak time. I would put money on the CDN. The handball launch added load too, but the stalls started two days before that.'
24	CATALOGUE (full contents)
25	C1 [stage S1] Tessaline Networks monthly service report, Kestria, October - Tessaline Networks account team (vendor-account): Tessaline service report, Varsk point of presence, October. Availability 99.995% (SLA 99.95%). Peak delivered throughput 412 Gbps against 900 Gbps provisioned capacity. Cache hit ratio, month average 92.6%, 'consistent with normal warm-up after onboarding'. Origin fetch error rate 0.002%; HTTP 5xx rate 0.004%. 'All SLA metrics were met for the period. We are aware of customer-reported rebuffering and are happy to support the investigation, but our edge metrics do not indicate a delivery fault.'
26	C2 [stage S1] Playback telemetry for Kestria, 12–25 October, broken down by client app, app version and ISP - Player session beacon warehouse, query by data engineering (telemetry): Session beacons, Kestria, 12–25 Oct. All sessions served by Tessaline (beacon CDN field). Rebuffering ratio by client (share of Kestria viewing hours in brackets): smart-TV app 5.2 — 5.9% (40%); smart-TV app 5.1, devices with auto-update off — 0.7% (8%); web player — 0.6% (22%); iOS/Android apps, unchanged since September — 0.7% (30%). By ISP, smart-TV 5.2: Kestnet 5.9%, Ostral Telecom 5.8%, Brevi Fibre 6.0%; all other clients on each of those ISPs 0.6–0.7%. Same breakdown for 24 Sep–7 Oct (Corvane): every client and every ISP 0.5–0.7%. Median video start time, 12–25 Oct: smart-TV 5.2 1.5 s; all other clients 2.4 s. Note: ad hoc warehouse query. Store listings approved in all markets 8 Oct. Pre-release dogfood: 380 employee TVs in Dravia, served by Corvane, 24 Sep–8 Oct: rebuffering 5.7% on 5.2 versus 0.6% on 5.1. Ticket QA-2291: 'deferred until after general availability'.
28	C4 [stage S1] Random sample of 40 Kestria buffering tickets, 13–19 October - Customer support quality team (customer-account): Random sample of 40 tickets tagged buffering/playback. 30	C6 [stage S1] Kestria cancellation exit survey results, October - Subscriber lifecycle team (system-record): Optional exit survey shown at cancellation, Kestria, October. Share of viewing by device class unchanged across the period: smart TV 48%, mobile 30%, web 22%.
32	C8 [stage S1] CDN cutover execution log, CHG-4471, 8–9 October - Network operations runbook log (log): 8 Oct 22:00 DNS weight Tessaline 10%. 23:15 25%. 9 Oct 00:30 50%. 02:15 origin-shield HTTP 503 burst lasting 41 s, auto-recovered, 0.3% of requests in that minute affected. 03:20 75%. 04:10 100%. Health checks green throughout apart from 02:15. Post-cutover validation 04:30: test streams started successfully from Kestnet, Ostral and Brevi Fibre test lines. Change closed 05:05 by on-call network engineer.
33	C9 [stage S1] Synthetic probe results, Kestria, 1–31 October - Network monitoring platform (telemetry): Twelve probes (four per major ISP) fetch a fixed 6-second video segment every 5 minutes. 34	C10 [stage S1] Social media mention monitoring, Kestria, September–October - Brand monitoring agency (external-data): Mentions of Orvanta Play with negative playback terms: 380 in September, 2,940 in October. 35	C11 [stage S1] On-call incident channel transcript, Kestria playback, 9–12 October - Engineering chat export, incident INC-8812 (log): 9 Oct 21:40 alert: Kestria rebuffering > 1.5%. 21:52 'probably cold cache on the new CDN, give it a day.' 10 Oct 10:05 'Tessaline says hit ratio is climbing.' 10 Oct 22:30 'still 2.7%, handball starts tomorrow, expect worse.' 11 Oct 23:10 'no worse tonight, oddly.' 12 Oct 09:00 'escalated to vendor management.' 12 Oct 09:20 INC-8812 reassigned to Partnerships as a vendor issue; engineering on-call stood down.
36	C12 [stage S1] National regulator fixed-broadband speed statistics, Kestria, 2026 - Kestrian Communications Authority annual report (regulator-record): Kestrian Communications Authority, fixed broadband performance 2026. Median download speed 64 Mbps (2025: 61 Mbps). Lines below 10 Mbps: 11% (2025: 12%). Evening slowdown (median, 20:00–22:00 versus daily average): 7%. Three largest providers: Kestnet, Ostral Telecom, Brevi Fibre. No provider-level outages above 4 hours were recorded in September or October 2026.
37	C13 [stage S1] Kestria smart-TV app install base by manufacturer and model year - App analytics (system-record): Orvanta Play smart-TV installs in Kestria, 1 November: Halvik 34%, Sorenta 29%, Myra 18%, others 19%. Model years 2019–2025; median model year 2022. Manufacturer and model-year mix is within ±4 percentage points of Dravia and of the all-market average. Share of TVs with automatic app updates switched off: 14%.
38	C14 [stage S1] Video encoding and packaging change log, September–October - Media pipeline change log (change-record): Encoding ladder: 8 renditions from 0.4 to 12 Mbps, unchanged since 3 June. Segment duration: 6 seconds, unchanged. Packaging changes in the period: one, on 15 Sep — subtitle format update applied to all markets simultaneously. No encoding, DRM or manifest changes were made for Kestria specifically. No changes are scheduled before January.
39	C15 [stage S1] Interview with Kestria customer care team lead, 3 November - Operations review interview notes (manager-account): Team lead, Kestria customer care: 'Agents follow the playback script: clear the cache, restart the router, reinstall the app. Reinstalling doesn't help; people ring back. We added two agents in late October and average handle time went from six to nine minutes. We don't record device type unless the customer volunteers it. Morale is low; agents feel they have nothing useful to tell people.'
40	CANDIDATES
41	H1: The migration of Kestria traffic to the new CDN provider is causing the rise in buffering in Kestria.
42	H2: The October smart-TV app release is causing the rise in buffering in Kestria.
43	H3: Congestion in Kestrian internet service providers' networks or interconnects is causing the rise in buffering in Kestria.
44	H4: Extra viewing demand from the handball streaming launch is causing the rise in buffering in Kestria.
45	R1: Migration of Kestria traffic to the new CDN provider -> Rise in rebuffering in Kestria (causes)
46	R2: Roll-out of smart-TV app 5.2 in Kestria -> Rise in rebuffering in Kestria (causes)
47	R3: Rise in rebuffering in Kestria -> Rise in Kestria subscription cancellations in October (causes)
48	R4: Kestrian Handball League streaming launch -> Rise in rebuffering in Kestria (causes)
49	A1: Send Tessaline an SLA breach notice, withhold its October fees and move Kestria traffic back to Corvane.
50	A2: Revert the smart-TV app's adaptive-streaming behaviour in Kestria to the 5.1 settings and hold the wider 5.2 rollout until the playback regression is fixed.
51	A3: Offer every Kestrian subscriber who cancelled in October a free month to return, funded from the playback-incident budget on the basis that buffering drove the cancellation rise.
52	A4: Add app version and device type as standard breakdowns on the playback quality dashboard and its alerts.
53	A5: Mute the Kestria rebuffering alert until the dispute with the CDN provider is resolved.

55	Q1: hypothesis H1 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
56	Q2: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
57	Q3: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
58	Q4: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
59	Q5: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
60	Q6: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
61	Q7: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
62	Q8: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
63	Q9: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
64	Q10: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
65	Q11: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
66	Q12: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
67	Q13: action A5 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
68	Q14: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

answers.justification: From 12 to 25 Oct, every client except smart-TV 5.2 rebuffered at 0.6–0.7% on Tessaline, the same as before the switch (C2). The 5.2 regression also showed up on Corvane in the Dravia dogfood test (5.7% vs 0.6%, C3), and Tessaline met all its SLA metrics with plenty of spare capacity (C1).

Rebuffering is 5.9% on smart-TV 5.2 against 0.6–0.7% everywhere else, on every ISP (C2). The rise began on 9 Oct, when 5.2 rolled out to 100% of Kestria as the only canary market (C3, E3). 5.2 lowered its buffer targets (C3), and the same regression appeared on Corvane in Dravia (C3).

On Kestnet, Ostral and Brevi Fibre alike, only 5.2 sessions are elevated and all other clients stay at 0.6–0.7% (C2). Kestnet's interconnect raised no loss alarms (C5), and national broadband statistics are stable (C12).
Rebuffering rose on 9–10 Oct, before the 11 Oct handball launch (E3, E6). Match nights were no worse than other days (E3, C11), and other clients stayed flat despite the extra demand (C2, C7).

Non-5.2 clients served by Tessaline show unchanged rebuffering (C2), the regression reproduces on Corvane (C3), and the probe shifts are small (C9). That counts against the CDN link even though the timing coincides (E2).

The evidence has timing (C3, E3), a mechanism (lower buffer thresholds, C3), and covariation isolated to 5.2 within the same CDN and ISPs (C2). The Corvane dogfood replication (C3) rules out the CDN as the rival explanation.

Cancellations rose in the same month as buffering (E4, C6), but the 1 Oct price rise is a confounder (E4, C6, C4). The exit survey doesn't offer streaming quality as an answer and free-text replies weren't exported (C6).
The rise came before the 11 Oct launch, and match nights were no worse (E3, C11), so the extra demand (C7) didn't drive rebuffering.
It punishes a vendor that met its SLA (C1) for a fault in our own app (C2, C3), and moving back to Corvane wouldn't fix 5.2 buffering (C3 Dravia dogfood).
It targets the established cause (C2, C3), can be reverted server-side per market within about an hour (C3), and stops the regression spreading to all markets on 20 Nov (C3).
Its stated basis, that buffering drove the cancellation rise, isn't established given the price-rise confounder and an exit survey with no quality option (C6, E4).

The country-only dashboard (E3) hid a client-specific regression that only an ad hoc query found (C2), so this is a sound monitoring fix. It needs a pipeline rebuild of about six weeks (C2), though, so it comes second to the immediate fix (A2).
It would switch off a protective alert that correctly detected a real regression (C11, E3), on the basis of a misattributed cause (E4 vs C2, C3).
The client-level split (C2), release config (C3) and Corvane dogfood replication (C3) are enough to commit to reverting the abr_v2 settings, which is cheap and reversible (C3).

ambiguousItems: Q12: A4 could be 'preferred', since the monitoring gap is a root contributor to the misdiagnosis, or 'acceptable', since the six-week rebuild makes it secondary to the immediate A2 revert.
Q7: R3 could be 'unknown' rather than 'association-only', because the only temporal co-occurrence is confounded by the price rise and there is no individual-level link.
caseProblems: E5 says 5.2 is 'live in all markets', but C3's rollout gate shows 0% outside Kestria. This looks intentional (store approval vs rollout gate) and is plausible, not an error.
C3 bundles the decisive Dravia/Corvane dogfood result with the rollout configuration in one item, which makes the case very easy once C3 is read. It doesn't leak through its title, though.
The internal numbers are consistent: the C2 weighted mix (~2.75%) matches E3's 2.6–2.9%, and the C2 smart-TV share (48%) matches C7.
